slides.text: To pass the forty-minute commute on the midnight Red Line train, I sketch the strangers sitting across from me in charcoal. After a year, I had filled six leather sketchbooks with hundreds of anonymous faces. Tonight, an exhausted homicide detective sat beside me, glanced down at the portrait I was shading, and went pale. 'Where did you see this man?' he demanded.

'Right there,' I said, pointing across the aisle—except the seat under the flickering fluorescent tube was completely empty. The detective pulled a thick case file from his briefcase. The man I had just drawn was Thomas Kael, the first victim of the Red Line Strangler, pulled from the tracks three years ago. 'Is this some kind of sick joke?' the detective whispered, flipping backward through my sketchbook.

Page after page, the detective matched my charcoal commuters to every unsolved disappearance in the city over the last twelve months—until he reached the final page, which I had sketched ten minutes ago before he boarded. It was a drawing of the detective himself, slumped in the exact seat he was currently occupying, with a piano wire pulled taut around his collar from behind.
